title: Taste Is All That's Left
excerpt: On what is left to do once the machine can make anything, and why taste is the last craft worth keeping.
content_html:
For most of the time I have been writing software—which, compared to some of my readers, is not that long—I have come to believe that the hard thing was making the thing exist at all. This is not necessarily a new belief of mine. I started through the difficult and tedious experience of building web applications and watching them crash and burn.

You had an idea, and between the idea and the working program stood hours— sometimes weeks—of typing, of reading manuals, of misunderstanding an API and slowly grinding the wrong version into a slightly less wrong one. Production was the wall. Everyone hit it. It was the thing that separated the people who could from the people who could only talk about it.

That wall is gone. Or rather, it has been rented out. 1 You can describe a thing now and receive a plausible version of it much faster than you could have typed the first function by hand. The idea-to-artifact distance, the one that defined the entire craft, has collapsed to almost nothing.

Though, you have not been warned about one little thing: the value you built by learning to climb that wall does not disappear. It simply… moves.

The Bar Went Somewhere

We keep asking whether the machines are any good. Even yesterday I had a rather short discussion on whether they are reliable. While we have concluded that they are “reliably unreliable,” I think it is the wrong question. The output is good enough, generally anyway, and that is the problem—most of it, at least. Good enough is a solvent. It dissolves the reason to do better. For as long as making things was expensive, the expense did quiet work on our behalf. It rationed output. It meant that anything which existed had, at minimum, survived the cost of being made. You know what I mean? Effort was a filter, and like all filters it was invisible until it was removed. Nobody shipped a thousand mediocre variations of a feature, because a thousand mediocre variations cost a thousand times as much as one. The economics enforced a floor.

That floor is now gone. And when the floor goes, the thing that decides what is worth keeping is no longer the cost of making it. It is you. Your judgement. The verdict you reach when you look at three plausible versions of the same function and know, somehow, that two of them are wrong. That verdict has a name we are slightly embarrassed to use in engineering circles, because it sounds soft and unfalsifiable and vaguely aristocratic.

Taste.

What Taste Actually Is

I want to be careful here, because “taste” is doing a lot of work and it is easy to hear it as decoration. A matter of preferences. Whether you like your braces on the same line.

That is not what I mean.

Robert Pirsig spent an entire book circling a word he refused to define, because he had convinced himself that defining it would kill it. He called it Quality. His argument, roughly, was that you recognise Quality before you can explain it— that the recognition comes first and the reasons arrive later, if they arrive at all. A good mechanic knows the engine is wrong before he knows why. A good editor feels the sentence sag before she can name the clause that failed. 2

Taste is that. It is the compressed, wordless verdict you reach faster than you can justify. It is partially 3 the “no, again” you say to yourself with total conviction and no available argument. And it is not soft at all. It is the hardest thing in the work, because it is the only part that was never mechanical to begin with.

Everything downstream of the verdict—the typing, the syntax, the wiring of one library to another—was always, in principle, automatable. We just had not gotten around to it. The verdict was the thing the machine could not do for you.

It still cannot. It can only make the absence of it cheaper to ignore.

Taste Is Downstream of Friction

Here is the uncomfortable mechanism, the part I would rather not think about.

Where did your taste come from?

No really. Where did it come from, was it genetic? Were you abducted by aliens one day that forcefully injected your sense of taste into your mind and wiped your memory?

I’ll tell you this much: it’s not from consuming good work. You cannot read a hundred excellent programs and absorb the judgement by osmosis, any more than you can become a chef by eating in good restaurants. Taste is built the slow, stupid, humiliating way: you make something bad, you are forced to live with it, it fails in front of you, and some part of you files the failure away. Then you do it again. The palate is an accretion of your own mistakes, sat with long enough to sting.

The friction was not an obstacle to developing taste. The friction was the curriculum. Every wall I cursed while climbing it was, without my noticing, teaching me which walls were worth climbing. The cost that rationed my output also educated my judgement, because paying the cost over and over is how you learn what is worth paying for.

So watch what happens when you remove the friction for the next person.

They can generate fluently from the first day. They will never ship the bad version and be forced to sit in it, because the tool offers them a competent version for free. They will climb no wall, and so they will learn nothing from the climb. They will arrive at fluency having skipped the entire apprenticeship that fluency used to require—and they will be more productive than I was at their stage, by every metric anyone bothers to measure.

They will be able to make anything, and unable to tell (or stop to think) whether they should. Not necessarily through any fault of their own. We removed the part of the process that would have taught them, and we called it progress, and by most definitions it was.

The Economics Are Against You

Suppose you have taste. Suppose you paid the full price and you can feel the sag in the sentence and the wrongness in the function.

Congratulations! You now ship at exactly the same speed as the person who cannot.

This is the quiet cruelty of the situation and I do not have a comforting way to phrase it. Taste is slow. It says “no, again.” It sends the plausible thing back because plausible is not the same as right, and while it is doing that, the person without it has already shipped, closed the ticket, and moved on. The market timed you both with the same stopwatch and it did not see the difference. It cannot see the difference. Taste does not show up in the diff.

It is unmeasurable, uncreditable, and invisible on a dashboard. You cannot point to the disasters it prevented, because prevented disasters leave no trace. You carry a cost—the extra hours, the returned work, the refusal to ship the fine thing when the right thing is still reachable—and you carry it alone, against an incentive gradient that runs the other way.

Harry Frankfurt once drew a careful line between the liar and the bullshitter. The liar at least respects the truth enough to work against it. The bullshitter does not care about the truth in either direction; he is simply indifferent to it. 4 Slop is the bullshit of engineering. It is not wrong, exactly. It is indifferent. It works, it passes, it is fine. And fine, produced without friction and shipped without judgement, is now the most abundant substance in the field.

The Flood

Sturgeon said it decades ago, defending science fiction from a critic: ninety percent of everything is crap. 5 He meant it as consolation. Ninety percent of every field is bad, so do not judge the field by its bulk. But the ratio was never the danger. It held steady for centuries. What held the flood back was that producing the crap cost something. Bad novels still took a year to write. Bad software still took a month to build. The ninety percent was throttled at the source by the sheer inconvenience of making it.

We have now removed the throttle and left the ratio intact. Ninety percent of an infinite output is still infinite. The signal did not get worse. The noise became free, and free noise rises without limit, and every real thing you make now arrives into a sea of plausible nothing that looks, at a glance, exactly like it.

Which means the scarce act is no longer making. It is choosing. Deciding what, out of the endless generated plausible, deserves to exist and be kept. Curation was a minor virtue when things were expensive to make. It is the whole game when they are free.

What Deserves to Exist

There is a rhyme here, if you go back far enough.

When the factories came, they could suddenly make everything—cheaply, uniformly, by the thousand. 6 And a handful of people, Morris and Ruskin among them, looked at the flood of cheap identical goods and asked a question that sounded, at the time, sentimental and doomed: not can we make this, but should this be made, and made this way, by no one, for no reason but that the machine could.

They lost the economic argument. They were always going to. But they were right about the thing that mattered, which is that when the making becomes free, the choosing becomes the craft. The human question stops being “can I build it” and becomes “does this deserve to exist”—and that question was always the more serious one. We just could not afford to ask it while we were busy climbing walls.

I keep coming back to this turn. It is not consolation but a correction.

The tools did not devalue the skill. They stripped away everything that was not the skill. All those years I thought the work was the production—the typing, the wiring, the wall—and production turns out to have been the toll. The tax you paid for the privilege of exercising judgement. Now the tax is close to zero, and what is left standing, exposed, with nowhere to hide, is the judgement itself. The part that was always the point.

Taste did not become less valuable. It became the only thing that was ever scarce. We just could not see it, because it was buried under all the labour it used to take to get to it.

A Defense, Then

So here is the defense, such as it is.

Anyone can generate now. That race is over and it was never worth winning. The discipline that remains—the one the machine cannot rent you and the dashboard cannot see—is in the deletion. In the “no, again.” In caring about the difference between fine and right when nothing external will ever reward you for caring, when the market has timed you and shrugged, when the plausible version sits there working and passing and asking only to be let through.

Refuse it anyway. Not out of nostalgia for the friction—I do not miss the wall, and I will not pretend to. Refuse it because the verdict is the last part of this that is actually yours. It is unmeasurable, which means no one can take it from you by measuring it. It is unautomatable, which means no one can sell it back to you. It is slow, which in a field optimising for infinite speed is starting to look less like a handicap and more like the only remaining evidence that a human was here and gave a damn.

Everyone can make anything. Almost no one can tell you what is worth making.

That was always the harder skill. It is now the only one left.

Post-Mortem

On Language

This post reads off as AI slop. You said it, I see it. I’m sincerely sorry for publishing something that has allowed you to feel this way. If my word means anything to you, I would like to assure you that this post was not authored by a LLM. Nor was it storyboarded, reviewed, checked, etc. by a LLM. Some readers have pointed out that people do not speak this way. That is correct. I do not speak, nor usually write, like this and this post will go down as my not-the-proudest, however, I take your criticism to heart—although not personally—and strive to improve.

I do write like this sometimes. The short sentences, the reversals, the one-word lines—all of it. It’s just the way it is. A LLM writes that way too, because it was trained on the same essays I grew up reading, so me doing it badly and a machine doing it look about the same to you on the page. That says something about my writing. It says nothing about who wrote it.

So let me be plain about it: Claude was not here. No LLM wrote this—not a sentence of it, nor was it outlined, drafted, reviewed, checked, etc. by one, and there is no prompt behind it either. It is just me, writing worse than usual. I will write the next one plainer. Next time, write to me. I too am a person behind this screen.

In Appreciation

Be assured that I have read all of your comments—the good and the bad. As with my previous post that reached Hacker News, I’ve received many insightful ones. Whether it was people sharing their experience, or negative comments with the decency to criticize with substance, I have learned something new today—for which I am thankful.

On Taste

I do not care about your taste. If this posts has offended you, then it tells more about you than it does about me. As they say, “throw an insult on the ground, its owner will pick it up”—this one I am not sorry about.

blocks.html_en: We keep asking whether the machines are any good. Even yesterday I had a rather short discussion on whether they are reliable. While we have concluded that they are “reliably unreliable,” I think it is the wrong question. The output is good enough, generally anyway, and that is the problem—most of it, at least. Good enough is a solvent. It dissolves the reason to do better. For as long as making things was expensive, the expense did quiet work on our behalf. It rationed output. It meant that anything which existed had, at minimum, survived the cost of being made. You know what I mean? Effort was a filter, and like all filters it was invisible until it was removed. Nobody shipped a thousand mediocre variations of a feature, because a thousand mediocre variations cost a thousand times as much as one. The economics enforced a floor.

blocks.html_en: Robert Pirsig spent an entire book circling a word he refused to define, because he had convinced himself that defining it would kill it. He called it Quality. His argument, roughly, was that you recognise Quality before you can explain it— that the recognition comes first and the reasons arrive later, if they arrive at all. A good mechanic knows the engine is wrong before he knows why. A good editor feels the sentence sag before she can name the clause that failed. 2

blocks.html_en: Taste is that. It is the compressed, wordless verdict you reach faster than you can justify. It is partially 3 the “no, again” you say to yourself with total conviction and no available argument. And it is not soft at all. It is the hardest thing in the work, because it is the only part that was never mechanical to begin with.

sentences.en: Taste is that.

sentences.en: It is partially 3 the “no, again” you say to yourself with total conviction and no available argument.

sentences.en: And it is not soft at all.

blocks.html_en: I’ll tell you this much: it’s not from consuming good work. You cannot read a hundred excellent programs and absorb the judgement by osmosis, any more than you can become a chef by eating in good restaurants. Taste is built the slow, stupid, humiliating way: you make something bad, you are forced to live with it, it fails in front of you, and some part of you files the failure away. Then you do it again. The palate is an accretion of your own mistakes, sat with long enough to sting.

blocks.html_en: Sturgeon said it decades ago, defending science fiction from a critic: ninety percent of everything is crap. 5 He meant it as consolation. Ninety percent of every field is bad, so do not judge the field by its bulk. But the ratio was never the danger. It held steady for centuries. What held the flood back was that producing the crap cost something. Bad novels still took a year to write. Bad software still took a month to build. The ninety percent was throttled at the source by the sheer inconvenience of making it.

blocks.html_en: There is a rhyme here, if you go back far enough.

sentences.en: There is a rhyme here, if you go back far enough.
sentences.zh: 如果你回溯得足够远的话，这里有一个韵律。

blocks.html_en: When the factories came, they could suddenly make everything—cheaply, uniformly, by the thousand. 6 And a handful of people, Morris and Ruskin among them, looked at the flood of cheap identical goods and asked a question that sounded, at the time, sentimental and doomed: not can we make this, but should this be made, and made this way, by no one, for no reason but that the machine could.

sentences.en: When the factories came, they could suddenly make everything—cheaply, uniformly, by the thousand.
sentences.zh: 当工厂到来时，他们突然可以制造一切——廉价、统一、批量生产。

sentences.en: 6 And a handful of people, Morris and Ruskin among them, looked at the flood of cheap identical goods and asked a question that sounded, at the time, sentimental and doomed: not can we make this, but should this be made, and made this way, by no one, for no reason but that the machine could.
sentences.zh: 6 包括莫里斯和拉斯金在内的一小群人看着大量廉价的相同商品，问了一个在当时听起来伤感又注定的问题：我们不能制造这个，但应该制造这个，并且以这种方式制造，没有人，没有任何理由，除了机器可以。

blocks.html_en: They lost the economic argument. They were always going to. But they were right about the thing that mattered, which is that when the making becomes free, the choosing becomes the craft. The human question stops being “can I build it” and becomes “does this deserve to exist”—and that question was always the more serious one. We just could not afford to ask it while we were busy climbing walls.

sentences.en: They lost the economic argument.
sentences.zh: 他们在经济争论上失败了。

sentences.en: They were always going to.
sentences.zh: 他们总是会这么做。

sentences.en: But they were right about the thing that mattered, which is that when the making becomes free, the choosing becomes the craft.
sentences.zh: 但他们在重要的事情上是正确的，那就是当制作变得自由时，选择就变成了手艺。

sentences.en: The human question stops being “can I build it” and becomes “does this deserve to exist”—and that question was always the more serious one.
sentences.zh: 人类的问题不再是“我能建造它吗”，而是变成“这是否值得存在”——而这个问题总是更严肃的问题。

sentences.en: We just could not afford to ask it while we were busy climbing walls.
sentences.zh: 当我们忙着爬墙时，我们根本没能力问这个问题。

blocks.html_en: I keep coming back to this turn. It is not consolation but a correction.

sentences.en: I keep coming back to this turn.
sentences.zh: 我不断地回到这个回合。

sentences.en: It is not consolation but a correction.
sentences.zh: 这不是安慰，而是纠正。

blocks.html_en: The tools did not devalue the skill. They stripped away everything that was not the skill. All those years I thought the work was the production—the typing, the wiring, the wall—and production turns out to have been the toll. The tax you paid for the privilege of exercising judgement. Now the tax is close to zero, and what is left standing, exposed, with nowhere to hide, is the judgement itself. The part that was always the point.

sentences.en: The tools did not devalue the skill.
sentences.zh: 这些工具并没有贬低技能的价值。

sentences.en: They stripped away everything that was not the skill.
sentences.zh: 他们剥夺了一切不属于技能的东西。

sentences.en: All those years I thought the work was the production—the typing, the wiring, the wall—and production turns out to have been the toll.
sentences.zh: 那些年来，我一直以为工作就是生产——打字、布线、修墙——结果结果是生产造成了损失。

sentences.en: The tax you paid for the privilege of exercising judgement.
sentences.zh: 您为行使判断权而缴纳的税款。

sentences.en: Now the tax is close to zero, and what is left standing, exposed, with nowhere to hide, is the judgement itself.
sentences.zh: 现在税收接近于零，剩下的就是判决本身，暴露在外，无处可藏。

sentences.en: The part that was always the point.
sentences.zh: 这部分始终是重点。

blocks.html_en: Taste did not become less valuable. It became the only thing that was ever scarce. We just could not see it, because it was buried under all the labour it used to take to get to it.

sentences.en: Taste did not become less valuable.
sentences.zh: 品味并没有变得不那么有价值。

sentences.en: It became the only thing that was ever scarce.
sentences.zh: 它成为唯一稀缺的东西。

sentences.en: We just could not see it, because it was buried under all the labour it used to take to get to it.
sentences.zh: 我们只是看不到它，因为它被过去需要付出的所有劳动所掩埋。

blocks.html_en: Anyone can generate now. That race is over and it was never worth winning. The discipline that remains—the one the machine cannot rent you and the dashboard cannot see—is in the deletion. In the “no, again.” In caring about the difference between fine and right when nothing external will ever reward you for caring, when the market has timed you and shrugged, when the plausible version sits there working and passing and asking only to be let through.

sentences.en: Anyone can generate now.
sentences.zh: 现在任何人都可以生成。

sentences.en: That race is over and it was never worth winning.
sentences.zh: 那场比赛已经结束了，它从来不值得获胜。

sentences.en: The discipline that remains—the one the machine cannot rent you and the dashboard cannot see—is in the deletion.
sentences.zh: 剩下的纪律——机器不能租给你、仪表板也看不到的纪律——正在被删除。

sentences.en: In the “no, again.”
sentences.zh: 在“不，再来一次”中。

sentences.en: In caring about the difference between fine and right when nothing external will ever reward you for caring, when the market has timed you and shrugged, when the plausible version sits there working and passing and asking only to be let through.
sentences.zh: 在关心好与正确之间的区别时，当任何外部因素都不会奖励你的关心时，当市场已经为你计时并耸耸肩时，当合理的版本坐在那里工作、通过并要求只是让你通过时。

blocks.html_en: Refuse it anyway. Not out of nostalgia for the friction—I do not miss the wall, and I will not pretend to. Refuse it because the verdict is the last part of this that is actually yours. It is unmeasurable, which means no one can take it from you by measuring it. It is unautomatable, which means no one can sell it back to you. It is slow, which in a field optimising for infinite speed is starting to look less like a handicap and more like the only remaining evidence that a human was here and gave a damn.

sentences.en: Refuse it anyway.
sentences.zh: 无论如何都要拒绝。

sentences.en: Not out of nostalgia for the friction—I do not miss the wall, and I will not pretend to.

blocks.html_en: This post reads off as AI slop. You said it, I see it. I’m sincerely sorry for publishing something that has allowed you to feel this way. If my word means anything to you, I would like to assure you that this post was not authored by a LLM. Nor was it storyboarded, reviewed, checked, etc. by a LLM. Some readers have pointed out that people do not speak this way. That is correct. I do not speak, nor usually write, like this and this post will go down as my not-the-proudest, however, I take your criticism to heart—although not personally—and strive to improve.

blocks.html_en: • There is an older word for this arrangement. You no longer own the means of production; you rent them, by the token, from whoever trained the model. An English teacher of mine—a committed socialist—would have had the whole thing diagrammed on the board before I finished the sentence: the worker separated first from his tools, then from the labour itself, then sold a frictionless substitute for the labour and told this was liberation. blocks.html_en: • Someone will (and has!) object that taste is not only the “no, again”—that compressing it to a verdict makes the work sound like leaning back in a chair and rejecting things while the machine does the labour. The objection is fair, which is why the sentence above says partially. The “no, again” is the shorthand, not the whole of it. The verdict lives inside the work—in the data structures that have to actually scale, in the privacy you have to actually mean, in the function you rewrite a fourth time because the third was merely fine. Taste is not the chair you lean back in. It is the reason you lean forward into all the rest of it. ↩

content_html_zh:
我大部分时间都在编写软件——与我的一些读者相比，时间并没有那么长——我开始相信，最困难的是让这个东西存在。 这不一定是我的新信念。 我首先经历了构建 Web 应用程序的困难而乏味的经历，然后看着它们崩溃和烧毁。

你有了一个想法，在这个想法和工作程序之间需要花费几个小时（有时是几周）的打字、阅读手册、误解 API 并慢慢地将错误的版本磨成一个稍微不那么错误的版本。 生产是一堵墙。 大家都击中了。 正是这一点将有能力的人和只能谈论的人区分开来。

那堵墙已经消失了。 或者更确切地说，它已经出租了。 1 您现在可以描述一个事物，并获得它的合理版本，这比您手动输入第一个函数要快得多。 想法与产品之间的距离，即定义整个飞行器的距离，已经几乎消失得无影无踪。

尽管如此，你并没有被警告过一件小事：你通过学习攀登那堵墙而建立的价值并没有消失。 它只是…… 移动。

酒吧去了某个地方

我们一直在问这些机器是否好用。 甚至昨天我就他们是否可靠进行了相当简短的讨论。 虽然我们得出的结论是它们“确实不可靠”，但我认为这是一个错误的问题。 无论如何，一般来说，输出已经足够好了，这就是问题所在——至少是大部分问题。 足够好的溶剂。 它消除了做得更好的理由。 只要制造东西的成本很高，这笔费用就对我们无声无息地起作用。 它实行产量配给制。 这意味着任何存在的东西至少都在制造成本中幸存下来。 你知道我的意思？ 努力是一个过滤器，就像所有的过滤器一样，它在被移除之前是不可见的。 没有人会发布某个功能的一千个平庸变体，因为一千个平庸变体的成本是一个的一千倍。 经济因素强制规定了下限。

那层楼现在已经没有了。 当地板消失时，决定什么值得保留的不再是制造它的成本。 是你。 你的判断。 当您查看同一函数的三个看似合理的版本并且以某种方式知道其中两个是错误的时，您会得出这样的结论。 这个判决有一个我们在工程界使用起来有点尴尬的名字，因为它听起来很柔和、不可证伪，而且隐约带有贵族气息。

Taste.

味道到底是什么

我在这里要小心，因为“品味”做了很多工作，而且很容易将其听作装饰。 偏好问题。 您是否喜欢牙套在同一条线上。

我不是这个意思。

罗伯特·波西格用整本书的篇幅围绕着一个他拒绝定义的词，因为他说服自己定义它会杀死它。 他称之为质量。 粗略地说，他的论点是，在你能够解释质量之前，你先认识到质量——认识先出现，而原因则稍后出现，如果它们真的出现的话。 一个好的机械师在知道原因之前就知道发动机出了问题。 一位优秀的编辑在说出失败的条款之前就会感觉到句子已经下垂了。 2

味道就是这样。 这是一个压缩的、无言的结论，你比你能证明的速度更快地得出了这个结论。 这部分是3你对自己说的“不，再一次”，你完全确信，没有任何可用的论据。 而且一点也不软。 这是工作中最困难的事情，因为它是唯一从一开始就不是机械的部分。

原则上，判决下游的所有内容（打字、语法、一个库到另一个库的连接）总是可自动化的。 我们只是还没有抽出时间去做这件事。 结论是机器无法为你做这件事。

还是不行。 它只会让它的缺失变得更容易被忽视。

味觉是摩擦的下游

这是令人不舒服的机制，我宁愿不去想这部分。

你的品味从何而来？

真的不。 它从哪里来，是遗传的吗？ 你是否有一天被外星人绑架，强行将你的味觉注入你的大脑并抹去你的记忆？

我告诉你这么多：这不是来自消耗好的工作。 你不可能读完一百个优秀节目并通过潜移默化吸收判断，就像你不可能通过在好餐馆吃饭而成为一名厨师一样。 品味是通过缓慢、愚蠢、羞辱的方式建立起来的：你做了一些糟糕的东西，你被迫忍受它，它在你面前失败了，而你的某些部分将失败归档。 然后你再做一次。 味觉是你自己错误的积累，坐得足够久就会刺痛。

摩擦并不是品味发展的障碍。 摩擦在于课程。 我在攀登时咒骂的每一堵墙，在我不知不觉中，都在告诉我哪些墙值得攀登。 限制我产出的成本也影响了我的判断，因为一遍又一遍地付出成本才能让你知道什么是值得付出的。

因此，请注意当您消除下一个人的摩擦时会发生什么。

他们从第一天就可以流畅地生成。 他们永远不会发布糟糕的版本并被迫使用它，因为该工具免费为他们提供了一个合格的版本。 他们不会攀登任何墙壁，因此他们不会从攀登中学到任何东西。 他们将跳过流利度所要求的整个学徒期，从而达到流利程度，并且从任何人都费心去衡量的每一个指标来看，他们将比我在他们的阶段更有生产力。

他们将能够创造任何东西，但却无法判断（或停下来思考）他们是否应该这样做。 不一定是因为他们自己的过错。 我们删除了过程中本来可以教会他们的部分，我们称之为进步，根据大多数定义，它确实是进步。

经济学对你不利

假设你有品味。 假设你付了全价，你能感觉到句子的下垂和功能的错误。

恭喜！ 现在，您的发货速度与无法发货的人完全相同。

这种情况是无声的残酷，我无法用一种令人安慰的方式来表达它。 味觉缓慢。 它说“不，再一次”。 它会发回看似合理的东西，因为合理与正确并不相同，而在它这样做的同时，没有它的人已经发货，关闭了票，然后继续前进。 市场用同一个秒表对你们俩进行计时，但它没有看到差异。 它看不出差异。 味道不会出现在差异中。

它是不可测量的、不可信的，并且在仪表板上是不可见的。 你无法指出它预防了哪些灾难，因为预防的灾难不会留下任何痕迹。 你要承担一定的成本——额外的工作时间、退回的工作、在正确的东西仍然可以到达时拒绝运送好东西——而且你独自承受它，反对相反的激励梯度。

哈里·法兰克福曾经在说谎者和胡言乱语者之间仔细地划出了界限。 说谎者至少足够尊重事实，可以与之对抗。 胡说八道者不关心任何一个方向的真相；他只是对此漠不关心。 4 Slop 是工程学的废话。 确切地说，这并没有错。 它是冷漠的。 它有效，它通过，很好。 而精细的产品，无摩擦生产，无评判运输，现在是该领域最丰富的物质。

洪水

几十年前，斯特金在为科幻小说免受批评家的攻击时说过这样的话：百分之九十的东西都是垃圾。 5 他的意思是为了安慰。 每个字段百分之九十都是坏的，所以不要以字段大小来判断字段。 但这个比例从来都不是危险。 几个世纪以来它一直保持稳定。 阻止洪水泛滥的原因是生产垃圾需要付出一定的代价。 烂小说还得花一年的时间才能写完。 糟糕的软件仍然需要一个月的时间来构建。 百分之九十的人都因为制作过程的不便而在源头上被扼杀了。

我们现在已经移除了油门并保持比例不变。 无限输出的百分之九十仍然是无限的。 信号并没有变差。 噪音变得自由，自由的噪音无限上升，你现在制作的每一件真实的东西都会进入一片看似合理的海洋，乍一看，它们看起来完全一样。

这意味着稀缺行为不再发生。 它正在选择。 从无穷无尽的看似合理的事物中决定什么值得存在和保留。 当制作成本高昂时，策展就成了次要的美德。 这是他们空闲时的整个游戏。

什么值得存在

如果你回溯得足够远的话，这里有一个韵律。

当工厂到来时，他们突然可以制造一切——廉价、统一、批量生产。 6 包括莫里斯和拉斯金在内的一小群人看着大量廉价的相同商品，问了一个在当时听起来伤感又注定的问题：我们不能制造这个，但应该制造这个，并且以这种方式制造，没有人，没有任何理由，除了机器可以。

他们在经济争论上失败了。 他们总是会这么做。 但他们在重要的事情上是正确的，那就是当制作变得自由时，选择就变成了手艺。 人类的问题不再是“我能建造它吗”，而是变成“这是否值得存在”——而这个问题总是更严肃的问题。 当我们忙着爬墙时，我们根本没能力问这个问题。

我不断地回到这个回合。 这不是安慰，而是纠正。

这些工具并没有贬低技能的价值。 他们剥夺了一切不属于技能的东西。 那些年来，我一直以为工作就是生产——打字、布线、修墙——结果结果是生产造成了损失。 您为行使判断权而缴纳的税款。 现在税收接近于零，剩下的就是判决本身，暴露在外，无处可藏。 这部分始终是重点。

品味并没有变得不那么有价值。 它成为唯一稀缺的东西。 我们只是看不到它，因为它被过去需要付出的所有劳动所掩埋。

防御，然后

所以这就是防御，就这样。

现在任何人都可以生成。 那场比赛已经结束了，它从来不值得获胜。 剩下的纪律——机器不能租给你、仪表板也看不到的纪律——正在被删除。 在“不，再来一次”中。 在关心好与正确之间的区别时，当任何外部因素都不会奖励你的关心时，当市场已经为你计时并耸耸肩时，当合理的版本坐在那里工作、通过并要求只是让你通过时。

无论如何都要拒绝。 并不是出于对摩擦的怀念——我并不想念那堵墙，我也不会假装想念。 拒绝它，因为判决是这件事的最后一部分，实际上是你的。 它是无法测量的，这意味着没有人可以通过测量来从你手中夺走它。 它是不可自动化的，这意味着没有人可以将其卖回给您。 它很慢，在一个针对无限速度进行优化的领域中，它开始看起来不再像一个障碍，而更像是唯一剩下的证据，证明人类曾经在这里并对此表示了该死的。

每个人都可以做任何事情。 几乎没有人能告诉你什么是值得做的。

这始终是更难的技能。 现在只剩下它了。

尸检

论语言

这篇文章读起来就像人工智能的废话。 你这么说，我都看出来了。 对于发布的内容让您有这样的感受，我深表歉意。 如果我的话对您有意义，我想向您保证这篇文章不是由法学硕士撰写的。 它也不是由法学硕士进行故事板、审查、检查等。 一些读者指出，人们不会这样说话。 这是正确的。 我不会像这样说话，也不会经常写文章，这篇文章将作为我最不自豪的文章而被记录下来，但是，我将您的批评铭记于心——尽管不是针对我个人的——并努力改进。

我有时确实会这样写。 短句、反转、单字台词——所有这些。 事情就是这样。 法学硕士也是这样写的，因为它是根据我从小到大阅读的相同论文进行训练的，所以我写得不好，而机器在页面上看起来和你写的差不多。 这说明了我的写作。 它没有说明是谁写的。

所以让我坦白地说：克劳德不在这里。 没有法学硕士写过这篇文章——不是其中的一句话，也不是由一个人概述、起草、审查、检查等，而且后面也没有任何提示。 只有我，写得比平时差。 下一篇我会写得更通俗一些。 下次，写信给我。 我也是这个屏幕后面的人。

赞赏

请放心，我已经阅读了您的所有评论——好的和坏的。 正如我之前在 Hacker News 上发表的文章一样，我收到了许多富有洞察力的文章。 无论是人们分享他们的经验，还是有礼貌地进行实质性批评的负面评论，我今天学到了一些新东西 - 对此我很感激。

口味上

我不在乎你的品味。 如果这篇文章冒犯了您，那么它更多地介绍了您而不是我。 正如他们所说，“把侮辱扔在地上，它的主人会把它捡起来”——对此我并不感到遗憾。
